title: Hepatitis B: Screening and Serology Interpretation

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult in primary care, an emergency department or a liver clinic who needs hepatitis B screening, interpretation of hepatitis B serology (HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HBc, HBeAg, anti-HBe, HBV DNA), classification into the five phases of chronic infection, pretreatment assessment, the decision to start antiviral treatment, prophylaxis before immunosuppression, pregnancy, exposure and vaccination, using the Saudi Association for the Study of Liver diseases and Transplantation (SASLT) 2021 update and 2014 guideline.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-18.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi Ministry of Health hepatitis B guideline was found open; the Saudi source used is the SASLT guideline (2021 update and the 2014 full guideline), so the authority is shown as Other.

The SASLT 2021 update gives no drug doses, and the dose tables in both papers were not extractable. Entecavir 0.5 mg (1 mg when lamivudine-resistant), tenofovir disoproxil 300 mg, lamivudine 100 mg and pegylated interferon alfa-2a 180 micrograms weekly are from the narrative of the 2014 guideline. The tenofovir alafenamide dose, renal dose adjustment table (2014 Table 8), the hepatitis B immunoglobulin dose and the vaccine dose and schedule for adults are not given in any source opened; check the product monograph and the Ministry of Health vaccination policy.

The SASLT texts do not describe IgM anti-HBc testing or how to tell acute from chronic infection by serology beyond 'HBsAg persisting more than 6 months indicates chronic infection'; acute hepatitis B is therefore described in outline only.

The 2021 SASLT update says anti-HBc alone cannot show immunity or chronic infection but gives no workup algorithm for isolated anti-HBc; the steps shown (repeat tests, HBV DNA, vaccination decisions) are limited to what the guideline implies and need specialist confirmation.

The 2014 guideline sets the Saudi upper limit of normal for ALT at 33 U/L for men and 22 U/L for women (study of Saudi liver donors) while the 2021 update uses ALT above about 40 IU/L for treatment; both are shown and local laboratory limits should be checked.
The 2014 text mentions old thresholds in copies/mL; only IU/mL values are used here. Some recommendation numbering in the 2014 text was lost in extraction.
Hepatitis D, hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance intervals, management of children and treatment-stopping rules in the 2021 update were only partly read and are mentioned briefly.
The Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) drug registration site could not be opened from this environment, so registration of each medicine was not verified; check hospital formulary.

Source texts were read through automated extraction of the open-access journal XML rather than page by page in the original, and the tables in both SASLT papers were not extractable, so each figure should be spot-checked against the source during clinical review.

pathophysiology.summary: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) spreads from mother to child at birth, between family members and through blood and injections; in Saudi Arabia perinatal and household transmission have been the main routes, and genotype D is the most common (SASLT 2014). Universal infant vaccination since 1989 to 1990 greatly lowered prevalence, so people aged about 28 years or younger are largely protected, but prevalence stays high in older adults, so people over 40 years are a screening target (SASLT 2014; SASLT 2021). HBsAg is the first marker to appear; HBsAg persisting beyond 6 months means chronic infection; anti-HBs follows recovery or vaccination and means immunity; anti-HBc shows past exposure but does not itself show immunity or chronic infection (SASLT 2014; SASLT 2021). Chronic infection runs through five phases defined by HBsAg/HBeAg, HBV DNA, ALT and liver inflammation: chronic infection HBeAg-positive (old name immune tolerant), chronic hepatitis HBeAg-positive, chronic infection HBeAg-negative (inactive carrier), chronic hepatitis HBeAg-negative, and resolved infection (SASLT 2021, Table 2). Patients with chronic infection, resolved infection or isolated anti-HBc can reactivate under immunosuppression or after hepatitis C direct-acting antivirals, and reactivation can be fatal (SASLT 2021; SASLT 2014).
keyMechanisms: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) spreads from mother to child at birth, between family members and through blood and injections; in Saudi Arabia perinatal and household transmission have been the main routes, and genotype D is the most common (SASLT 2014).

Universal infant vaccination since 1989 to 1990 greatly lowered prevalence, so people aged about 28 years or younger are largely protected, but prevalence stays high in older adults, so people over 40 years are a screening target (SASLT 2014; SASLT 2021).

HBsAg is the first marker to appear; HBsAg persisting beyond 6 months means chronic infection; anti-HBs follows recovery or vaccination and means immunity; anti-HBc shows past exposure but does not itself show immunity or chronic infection (SASLT 2014; SASLT 2021).

Chronic infection runs through five phases defined by HBsAg/HBeAg, HBV DNA, ALT and liver inflammation: chronic infection HBeAg-positive (old name immune tolerant), chronic hepatitis HBeAg-positive, chronic infection HBeAg-negative (inactive carrier), chronic hepatitis HBeAg-negative, and resolved infection (SASLT 2021, Table 2).

Patients with chronic infection, resolved infection or isolated anti-HBc can reactivate under immunosuppression or after hepatitis C direct-acting antivirals, and reactivation can be fatal (SASLT 2021; SASLT 2014).

symptoms: Most people are symptom free; discovery is by premarital, pre-employment, blood-donor, antenatal or abnormal-liver-test screening (SASLT 2021).
Acute hepatitis: jaundice, dark urine, fatigue, nausea, right upper abdominal discomfort.
Advanced disease: abdominal swelling, leg swelling, bleeding, confusion.
physicalSigns: Signs of chronic liver disease or splenomegaly (SASLT 2014, pretreatment examination).
Jaundice, ascites, encephalopathy or coagulopathy signal decompensation or acute liver failure.
redFlags: Jaundice with confusion, bleeding or prolonged prothrombin time: possible acute liver failure; admit and involve a liver unit, antiviral therapy is considered (SASLT 2014, symptomatic acute hepatitis B).

Cirrhosis or signs of decompensation (ascites, encephalopathy, variceal bleeding): start antiviral therapy immediately with early referral to a liver transplant centre, whatever the ALT or HBV DNA (SASLT 2014).

Patient about to start chemotherapy, rituximab or other anti-CD20 therapy, tumour necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitor, high-dose steroid or stem cell transplant: screen for HBsAg and anti-HBc and give prophylaxis before the first dose (SASLT 2021).

HBsAg-positive pregnant woman with HBV DNA above 100,000 IU/mL: start tenofovir at 24 to 28 weeks, and newborn needs hepatitis B immunoglobulin and vaccine within 12 hours of birth (SASLT 2021; SASLT 2014).
Needle-stick or contaminated blood or body-fluid exposure in a non-immune person: hepatitis B immunoglobulin and vaccine as soon as possible (SASLT 2021).
Flare of ALT after stopping or missing antivirals, or after hepatitis C direct-acting antiviral treatment: check HBV DNA and HBsAg, restart treatment (SASLT 2014; SASLT 2021).
precipitants: Immunosuppressive or cancer chemotherapy, especially anti-CD20 agents and high-dose steroids (SASLT 2021).
HIV or hepatitis C co-infection, dialysis, injection drug use (SASLT 2021, Table 3).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Shares risk factors; test every HBsAg-positive patient for HCV, HIV and HDV; usually one virus dominates and the dominant virus is treated first (SASLT 2014; SASLT 2021, Table 4).
Requires HBsAg to infect; suspect with unexplained ALT rise or severe hepatitis in an HBsAg-positive patient; confirmed by HDV antibody and RNA (SASLT 2014).

differentials.condition: Other chronic liver disease (alcohol, fatty liver, autoimmune liver disease)
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Screen for coexisting disease before antivirals; ALT may be raised from non-viral causes (SASLT 2014, pretreatment assessment).

differentials.condition: True inactive carrier versus HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Inactive carrier: HBV DNA below 2,000 IU/mL and normal ALT; HBeAg-negative hepatitis: fluctuating HBV DNA above 2,000 IU/mL with raised ALT; the two are sometimes hard to separate and need serial testing (SASLT 2021, Table 2).
Isolated anti-HBs with negative HBsAg and anti-HBc: vaccine-induced immunity (SASLT 2014; SASLT 2021).

ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Detects current infection; persisting more than 6 months means chronic infection (SASLT 2014).

clinicalManagement.title: First minutes: acute or decompensated presentation
actions: Jaundice with confusion, bleeding, ascites or prolonged prothrombin time: treat as decompensated liver disease or acute liver failure; admit under a liver unit with early contact with a liver transplant centre (SASLT 2014).
Send HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs, HBeAg, anti-HBe, HBV DNA, anti-HCV, HIV, anti-HDV, liver panel with prothrombin time, full blood count and creatinine (SASLT 2014; SASLT 2021, Table 4).
Start entecavir or tenofovir at once in decompensated cirrhosis even if HBV DNA is low, to prevent flare (SASLT 2014).
Never give interferon in decompensated cirrhosis or in acute hepatitis (SASLT 2014).

Symptomatic acute hepatitis B in a person who recovers spontaneously (over 95 to 99% of adults) needs no antiviral; antiviral therapy is for acute liver failure, continued until HBsAg clearance (SASLT 2014).

clinicalManagement.title: Who to screen and how to interpret the first result
actions: Screen the high-risk groups (pre-employment expatriates, health workers, contacts, dialysis, drug injectors, abnormal liver enzymes, pregnant women, inmates, people needing immunosuppression, HCV or HIV, donors) and consider adults over 40 years (SASLT 2021, Table 3).

Test HBsAg, anti-HBs and anti-HBc together: HBsAg positive means current infection (chronic if still positive after 6 months); HBsAg negative with anti-HBs 10 mIU/mL or more and anti-HBc negative means vaccine immunity; HBsAg negative with anti-HBc positive means resolved or occult infection and a reactivation risk under immunosuppression; all three negative means not immune, so vaccinate (SASLT 2014; SASLT 2021).

Isolated anti-HBc (HBsAg and anti-HBs negative) cannot by itself show immunity or infection: send HBV DNA and refer; give prophylaxis before anti-CD20, stem cell transplant, anti-TNF or checkpoint-inhibitor treatment (SASLT 2021; SASLT 2014 Recommendation 19).
Test sexual partners and first-degree relatives for HBsAg, anti-HBs and anti-HBc and vaccinate those negative for all (SASLT 2021).

clinicalManagement.title: Classify the phase of chronic infection
actions: Order HBeAg, anti-HBe, HBV DNA and ALT and place the patient in one of five phases (SASLT 2021, Table 2).
Phase 1 (chronic infection HBeAg-positive): HBeAg positive, HBV DNA above 10^7 IU/mL, normal ALT, no or minimal inflammation; highly contagious; no treatment in the absence of advanced disease.
Phase 2 (chronic hepatitis HBeAg-positive): HBeAg positive, HBV DNA 10^4 to 10^7 IU/mL, raised ALT, moderate or severe inflammation; consider treatment.
Phase 3 (chronic infection HBeAg-negative, inactive carrier): HBeAg negative, HBV DNA below 2,000 IU/mL, normal ALT; low risk; follow up.
Phase 4 (chronic hepatitis HBeAg-negative): HBeAg negative, fluctuating HBV DNA above 2,000 IU/mL, fluctuating or raised ALT, active inflammation; treat when criteria are met.
Phase 5 (resolved infection): HBsAg negative, anti-HBc positive, HBV DNA undetectable; reactivation risk under immunosuppression.

clinicalManagement.title: Pretreatment assessment
actions: History (family history of hepatitis B, cirrhosis or liver cancer, jaundice, injection drug use, vaccination including hepatitis A), examination for liver disease signs and splenomegaly, alcohol and herbal medicine advice (SASLT 2014).
Blood: liver enzymes, bilirubin, albumin, prothrombin time, full blood count including platelets, creatinine, HBV DNA, HBeAg and anti-HBe, anti-HCV, HIV, anti-HDV, anti-HAV (SASLT 2021, Table 4).

Liver ultrasound before treatment; fibrosis assessment by elastography, serum markers or biopsy when HBV DNA or ALT are borderline, and in patients over 40 years with mildly raised ALT (SASLT 2014; SASLT 2021).
Discuss the goal (long-term viral suppression to prevent cirrhosis and liver cancer), cost, adherence and the need for indefinite therapy in many patients (SASLT 2014).

clinicalManagement.title: Decide on treatment
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Once the phase and fibrosis are known
actions: Treat immediately: cirrhosis or decompensation, regardless of ALT, HBeAg status or HBV DNA (SASLT 2014).

Treat if HBeAg-positive with HBV DNA above 20,000 IU/mL and raised ALT for 3 to 6 months, or HBeAg-negative with HBV DNA above 2,000 IU/mL and raised ALT for 3 to 6 months, or significant inflammation or fibrosis on biopsy or non-invasive tests whatever the ALT (SASLT 2014, Recommendations 9 to 11).

2021 update: also treat HBV DNA above 2,000 IU/mL with ALT above the upper limit of normal and/or at least moderate necroinflammation or fibrosis; HBV DNA above 20,000 IU/mL with ALT above 2 times the upper limit may start without biopsy (SASLT 2021).

First-line: entecavir or tenofovir (disoproxil), as the most potent drugs with very low or no resistance (SASLT 2014, Recommendation 12); in the 2021 update tenofovir alafenamide is also used, preferred over tenofovir disoproxil where renal or bone disease is a concern (SASLT 2021).
Lamivudine-resistant virus: tenofovir; do not use entecavir (SASLT 2014, Recommendation 13).
Duration: HBeAg-positive, continue until 12 months after HBeAg seroconversion; HBeAg-negative, continue indefinitely or until HBsAg loss (SASLT 2014, Recommendations 14 and 15).
Pegylated interferon is an alternative in selected non-cirrhotic patients; avoid in pregnancy, decompensated cirrhosis and acute hepatitis (SASLT 2014).

clinicalManagement.title: Special populations
actions: Before chemotherapy or immunosuppression: screen HBsAg, anti-HBc and anti-HBs (and HBV DNA if HBsAg-positive); prophylaxis for all HBsAg-positive patients before the first dose; for HBsAg-negative anti-HBc-positive patients give prophylaxis if anti-CD20 therapy or stem cell transplant; continue at least 6 months after the last immunosuppressant, 12 months for anti-CD20; entecavir or tenofovir preferred, lamivudine and telbivudine avoided for long courses (SASLT 2021; SASLT 2014).

Pregnancy: screen all in the first trimester; if HBV DNA is above 100,000 IU/mL at 24 to 28 weeks start tenofovir (tenofovir alafenamide as alternative; lamivudine only if neither is available); switch entecavir, adefovir or interferon to tenofovir; delivery mode by obstetric indication; breastfeeding is not contraindicated once the infant has had immunoprophylaxis (SASLT 2021).
Newborn of an HBsAg-positive mother: hepatitis B immunoglobulin plus vaccine within 12 hours of birth (SASLT 2014, Recommendation).
HIV co-infection: start antiretroviral therapy regardless of CD4 count, with a tenofovir-based regimen; do not use lamivudine or entecavir alone as HBV monotherapy (SASLT 2021; SASLT 2014).

Hepatitis C direct-acting antivirals: treat HBV concurrently or before if criteria are met; monitor HBV DNA and ALT every 4 to 8 weeks during, and 3 months after, therapy; in HBsAg-negative anti-HBc-positive patients check ALT every 4 weeks (SASLT 2021).
Chronic kidney disease or dialysis: adjust dose by creatinine clearance; entecavir and lamivudine are safer than tenofovir and adefovir for the kidney (SASLT 2014).

clinicalManagement.title: Exposure, vaccination and contacts
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Within hours of exposure; routine thereafter
actions: Contaminated blood or body-fluid exposure in a non-immune person: hepatitis B immunoglobulin and hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible (SASLT 2021); doses are not given in SASLT, so follow the Ministry of Health policy.
Vaccinate all non-immune people at risk (HBsAg and anti-HBs negative); give hepatitis A vaccine to all people with chronic liver disease (SASLT 2014).

Check anti-HBs after the vaccine series in infants of infected mothers, health workers, dialysis patients and staff, immunocompromised people, those on chemotherapy and sexual partners; give a booster if below 10 mIU/mL; repeat the series if the first fails; no routine booster in immunocompetent people (SASLT 2021; SASLT 2014).
Counsel carriers: vaccinate household members, do not share razors or glucometers, cover wounds, clean blood spills, do not donate blood (SASLT 2021).

clinicalManagement.title: Monitoring
actions: On therapy: ALT, liver function and HBV DNA every 3 months at first, HBV DNA every 6 months once undetectable; check creatinine and phosphate regularly on tenofovir or adefovir (SASLT 2014, Recommendation 16).
After stopping: ALT and HBV DNA monthly for 3 months, then every 3 to 6 months (SASLT 2014).

Untreated HBeAg-positive: ALT every 3 months, HBV DNA every 6 to 12 months, fibrosis every 12 months; HBeAg-negative with HBV DNA below 2,000 IU/mL: ALT every 6 to 12 months and yearly HBV DNA and fibrosis assessment; HBV DNA at or above 2,000 IU/mL: ALT every 3 months in year one then every 6 months (SASLT 2021).

Virological breakthrough (rise of more than 1 log) is usually non-adherence or resistance: confirm adherence, test for mutations, and add a second drug without cross-resistance or switch (SASLT 2014).

regimens.indication: First-line treatment of chronic hepatitis B in treatment-naive adults, including cirrhosis; prophylaxis before immunosuppression
regimens.patientGroup: Adults with hepatitis B virus infection
regimens.dose: 0.5 mg once daily; 1 mg once daily only if lamivudine-resistant virus
regimens.duration: HBeAg-positive: until 12 months after HBeAg seroconversion; HBeAg-negative: indefinitely or until HBsAg loss; prophylaxis: at least 6 months after the last immunosuppressant (12 months after anti-CD20)
adjustments: Creatinine clearance below 50 mL/min: adjust the dose (SASLT 2014); Renal dose adjustment by creatinine clearance is given in Table 8 of the 2014 SASLT guideline, but the table body could not be extracted; the text only says the dose must be adjusted when creatinine clearance is below 50 mL/min (for entecavir) and to check the product monograph.
Pregnancy: US pregnancy category C; if discovered in pregnancy, switch to tenofovir (SASLT 2014; SASLT 2021).
Lamivudine-resistant disease: do not use entecavir; use tenofovir (SASLT 2014).
Hepatic and elderly adjustments are not stated in the SASLT texts; check the product monograph.
monitoring: HBV DNA every 3 months at first, every 6 months once undetectable; ALT and liver function every 3 months; creatinine (SASLT 2014, Recommendation 16).
contraindications: The SASLT guideline does not give a contraindication list for this medicine beyond the statements shown in the adjustments; check the product monograph.

Hepatic and elderly adjustments are not stated in the SASLT texts; check the product monograph.
monitoring: Creatinine clearance and phosphate every 3 months at first; bone health; HBV DNA and ALT as for entecavir (SASLT 2014).

monitoring: ALT every 3 months, HBV DNA every 6 months, HBeAg status yearly; after stopping review every 3 months (SASLT 2014).

medicationPlan.note: Doses are from the narrative of the 2014 SASLT guideline; the 2021 update gives no doses. Renal tables, tenofovir alafenamide dose, hepatitis B immunoglobulin and vaccine doses were not extractable and are flagged in the gaps. Initiation and monitoring rules are from the SASLT texts. The Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) drug registration site could not be opened from this environment, so registration of each medicine was not verified; check hospital formulary.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: HBsAg persisting more than 6 months (SASLT 2014, HBV diagnosis).
Anti-HBs 10 mIU/mL or more; booster advised when titre falls below 10 mIU/mL in health workers, dialysis, immunocompromised, partners and infants of infected mothers (SASLT 2021).

Expatriates (pre-employment), health workers, household and sexual contacts of carriers, dialysis patients, injection drug users, abnormal liver enzymes, pregnant women, inmates, people needing immunosuppression or chemotherapy, HCV or HIV positive, blood or organ donors, and adults over 40 years (SASLT 2021, Table 3).
HBV DNA above 20,000 IU/mL with raised ALT for 3 to 6 months (SASLT 2014, Recommendation 9).
HBV DNA above 2,000 IU/mL with raised ALT for 3 to 6 months (SASLT 2014, Recommendation 10).

HBV DNA above 2,000 IU/mL with ALT above the upper limit of normal and/or at least moderate necroinflammation or fibrosis; or HBV DNA above 20,000 IU/mL with ALT above 2 times the upper limit, without biopsy (SASLT 2021).

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Treat regardless of ALT or DNA

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Immune-tolerant (HBeAg-positive, normal ALT, high HBV DNA) or inactive carriers without advanced disease or family history of cirrhosis or liver cancer, especially if under 30 years; follow up (SASLT 2014).
All HBsAg-positive patients before treatment starts; HBsAg-negative but anti-HBc-positive patients if anti-CD20 therapy or stem cell transplant; also anti-TNF and checkpoint inhibitors (SASLT 2021).

teaching.scope: Adult in primary care, an emergency department or a liver clinic who needs hepatitis B screening, interpretation of hepatitis B serology (HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HBc, HBeAg, anti-HBe, HBV DNA), classification into the five phases of chronic infection, pretreatment assessment, the decision to start antiviral treatment, prophylaxis before immunosuppression, pregnancy, exposure and vaccination, using the Saudi Association for the Study of Liver diseases and Transplantation (SASLT) 2021 update and 2014 guideline.
learningObjectives: Interpret HBsAg, anti-HBs and anti-HBc together and classify the five phases.
Know when to treat, which drug to use and when to give prophylaxis.
Recognise pregnancy, immunosuppression and exposure scenarios that need action.
pitfalls: Treating immune-tolerant or inactive carriers without advanced disease.
Missing anti-HBc-positive patients before rituximab or stem cell transplant.
Using interferon in pregnancy or decompensated cirrhosis.
keyPoints: HBsAg positive beyond 6 months means chronic infection; anti-HBs 10 mIU/mL or more means immunity; anti-HBc alone does not show immunity.
Treat cirrhosis whatever the ALT or HBV DNA; thresholds are HBV DNA above 20,000 IU/mL (HBeAg-positive) and 2,000 IU/mL (HBeAg-negative) with raised ALT.
Screen for HBsAg and anti-HBc before any chemotherapy or immunosuppression and give prophylaxis; tenofovir at 24 to 28 weeks if HBV DNA above 100,000 IU/mL in pregnancy.

patientEducation: Hepatitis B can be controlled with daily tablets; do not stop them without your doctor because the infection can flare.
Family members and sexual partners should be tested and vaccinated.
Tell every doctor you have hepatitis B before chemotherapy, steroids or other immune-suppressing medicine.
Do not share razors, toothbrushes or glucose-testing equipment; cover cuts; do not donate blood.
If pregnant, tell your obstetrician; your baby needs immunoglobulin and vaccine within 12 hours of birth.
lifestyleAndDiet: Avoid alcohol and herbal remedies during treatment (SASLT 2014).
Healthy weight and balanced diet; vaccinate against hepatitis A if not immune.
mdtReferrals: Primary care physician; hepatologist or gastroenterologist; infectious diseases (HIV, HDV co-infection); obstetrician for pregnancy; oncologist or rheumatologist for prophylaxis before immunosuppression; nephrologist for dialysis; liver transplant centre for decompensation; clinical pharmacist.
dischargeCriteria: Discharge or manage at home when acute liver failure and decompensation are excluded, serology and HBV DNA are sent, the phase and treatment plan are documented, contacts are advised for testing and vaccination, and a hepatology review date is set.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Treated: ALT and HBV DNA every 3 months at first and HBV DNA every 6 months once undetectable, creatinine and phosphate on tenofovir; untreated HBeAg-positive: ALT every 3 months, HBV DNA every 6 to 12 months, fibrosis yearly; HBeAg-negative with HBV DNA below 2,000 IU/mL: ALT every 6 to 12 months, HBV DNA and fibrosis yearly; after stopping treatment monthly for 3 months then every 3 to 6 months; lifelong follow-up of all carriers.
